screens.title: Essential Game Algorithms
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will build an intuitive and practical understanding of three algorithm classes that appear everywhere in games: sorting, searching, and pathfinding. You will learn why choosing the right algorithm matters for performance, how to use C++ Standard Library tools like std::sort and std::binary_search, and the basic components that make A* effective for AI navigation. Expect concrete, game-focused examples: a leaderboard sorted by score, item lookup in an inventory, and a grid-based heuristic for pathfinding. We'll explain both the mechanics and the common pitfalls so you can avoid costly mistakes like sorting every frame or using an inadmissible heuristic. By the end you will know which algorithm to reach for, how to use standard library helpers safely, and what to measure when performance becomes a concern. As you move forward, keep an eye out for the hands-on activity that walks through a ready-to-run leaderboard and binary-search inventory check — that practical step will cement these ideas.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Essential Game Algorithms
Essential Game Algorithms
Sorting, searching, and pathfinding power leaderboards, inventories, and AI movement.
This lesson explains practical uses and shows how to use std::sort, std::find, std::binary_search, and the A* concept in grid-based games. Expect code examples and a hands-on activity to practice.
In this lesson
Understand algorithm roles and apply standard C++ helpers in game scenarios.
Coming up
A practical leaderboard example and a guide to A* components and heuristics.
Visual concept
Sorting: order items for display and processing
Searching: find items quickly when needed
Pathfinding: guide AI from A to B efficiently
Explore Key Topics
Sorting with std::sort
Use introsort-backed std::sort for O(N log N) ordering in leaderboards and rendering.
Linear vs Binary Search
Pick linear search for unsorted, binary for sorted collections to save comparisons.
A* and Heuristics
Learn g, h, and f costs and admissible heuristics like Manhattan distance for grids.

screens.title: What you will learn — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: This first objectives slide lays out the core practical skills you'll gain. First, you will understand why efficient sorting and searching matter in games. Knowing when to use a sorted collection versus a linear scan prevents costly frame-time spikes and improves responsiveness in leaderboards, rendering decisions, and inventory lookups. Second, you'll learn to use std::sort, including how to supply custom comparisons or operator overloads so complex objects like player records are sorted correctly. That skill saves time compared to hand-rolled sorts and leverages optimized introsort behavior. Third, you will differentiate linear search and binary search: you'll learn each algorithm's requirements, their typical time complexity, and scenarios where one clearly beats the other. Finally, you'll gain a conceptual grasp of pathfinding basics: open and closed lists, g-cost, h-cost, and f-cost, plus why heuristics like Manhattan distance are useful in grid-based worlds. Each objective is paired with a small competency milestone so you can verify you've achieved the skill in a practical way.

screens.title: What is an algorithm in games?
screens.narratorSegment: An algorithm is simply a defined set of steps for solving a problem. In games, algorithms appear in many forms: ordering a leaderboard, searching an inventory, or choosing a path for an NPC. The key is that an algorithm specifies how inputs are processed to produce outputs. For example, when you display a leaderboard you take an unsorted list of player scores as input and produce a sorted list from highest to lowest as output. That transformation is an algorithmic process. A common misconception is that algorithms are only academic. In practice, they directly affect player experience because they determine C P U usage and latency. Another misconception is that hand-rolled implementations are always better; standard library algorithms are often faster and more robust than ad-hoc code because they are implemented and tuned for general performance. Concrete example: sorting N scores using std::sort produces an ordered vector suitable for display and rank calculations. Takeaway: treating common game tasks as algorithmic problems lets you pick proven tools that keep your code predictable and fast. What small systems in your game would you treat as algorithms first?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › What is an algorithm in games?
Definition
A step-by-step procedure for transforming inputs into outputs. In games, this means tasks like sorting scores, finding items, or computing a path.
Example: Sorting a list of player scores to produce a leaderboard display.
Misconception: "I can write a quick sort faster than the standard library." Often std::sort is faster and safer.
Why it matters: Algorithms determine CPU cost and frame-time impact.
Key Takeaway

Treat common game behaviors as algorithmic problems. Then choose the right tool — standard library implementations are usually your first stop.

Concrete scenario
You need to display the top ten players each time a match ends. Algorithmic choice: sort scores on score change, not every frame. That keeps CPU use low while guaranteeing correct ranks.
Check your understanding
  • Identify three places in your game where an algorithm controls performance.
  • Decide whether a library algorithm or a custom scan is the right tool.
Common mistake
Running expensive algorithms like sorts inside the main render loop when the data hasn't changed.

screens.title: Sorting in games: uses and patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Sorting arranges elements into a specific order and plays a surprisingly large role in game systems. Typical uses include leaderboards that present top players, inventory screens that group and order items, rendering transparent objects back to front for correct blending, and optimizing collision broad-phase by sorting bounding boxes along an axis. Each of these examples has different constraints. Leaderboards demand a clear order by score; inventories may need stable ordering by type then name; rendering requires ordering by depth; collision systems often prefer sorts that expose nearby objects for quick elimination. A common error is to assume all tasks need the same sort behavior. Stable sorts preserve relative order of equal keys, which matters when secondary ordering is required. Performance matters: comparison-based sorts have a lower bound of O(N log N) on average, and std::sort implements a tuned hybrid commonly giving that performance in practice. Example: sort a vector of renderable objects by depth once per frame only if camera or object positions changed. Misconception to watch: sorting a very small list repeatedly costs less than complex caching, but for large collections avoid repeated full sorts. Takeaway: pick the right sort strategy and frequency for each game system to balance correctness and cost.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Sorting in games
Where sorting helps
Common in leaderboards, inventory organization, rendering order, and collision broad-phase optimization.
Leaderboard: sort by score descending to display top players.
Inventory: sort by category then name; use stable ordering if secondary order matters.
Rendering: sort transparent objects by depth for correct blending.
Collision: sorting bounding boxes along an axis speeds broad-phase checks.
Practical pattern
  1. Detect when data changes in a meaningful way.
  2. Sort once after the change, not continuously every frame.
  3. Prefer standard library sorts like std::sort for performance and correctness.
Key caution
Sorting large collections every frame can be a severe bottleneck; instead update order only on changes or use incremental structures.
Key Takeaway

Choose when to sort and which sort properties matter for correctness; this reduces unnecessary CPU work while keeping behavior predictable.

screens.title: Using std::sort safely and effectively
screens.narratorSegment: std::sort is the go-to C++ library function for ordering collections because it is highly optimized and typically implements an introsort: a hybrid of quicksort, heapsort, and insertion sort. The result is an algorithm that keeps average-case complexity near O(N log N) while avoiding pathological cases that can appear in simple quicksort implementations. In practical terms, that means you can rely on std::sort for most game collections: vectors of primitive values, objects with custom comparison operators, and containers where you can obtain random-access iterators. Consider the numbers and PlayerScore examples from the chapter. The numbers vector sorts in ascending order with a simple call, while PlayerScore provides either an operator< or a lambda comparator to produce descending score order. A common mistake is sorting inside a tight loop or on every frame. A better pattern is to call std::sort when data changes — for example, when a score updates, insert or update the entry and then sort if needed. Concrete example: use operator< inside PlayerScore to define default ordering for std::sort, or pass a lambda when a temporary ordering is needed. Takeaway: prefer std::sort for reliable performance and only sort when necessary.

keyIdea.title: Prefer std::sort
keyIdea.text: std::sort is a robust, high-performance choice for most game sorting needs; avoid needless repeated sorting.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › std::sort: code walkthrough
Example code
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
#include <string>

struct PlayerScore {
  std::string name;
  int score;
  bool operator<(const PlayerScore& other) const {
    return score > other.score; // Higher score first
  }
};

std::vector<int> numbers = {5,2,8,1,9,4};
std::sort(numbers.begin(), numbers.end()); // ascending

std::vector<PlayerScore> leaderboard = {{"Alice",1500},{"Bob",2000}};
std::sort(leaderboard.begin(), leaderboard.end()); // uses operator<
Note: HTML entities < and > are used in code blocks to keep syntax correct in rendered HTML.
Explanation
  • std::sort typically uses an introsort hybrid to guarantee O(N log N) average performance.
  • Provide operator< or a lambda comparator to control custom object ordering.
  • Sort only when the collection changes, not every frame.
Common mistake
Sorting thousands of elements every frame instead of sorting once when items change.
Key Takeaway

Use std::sort and custom comparators for reliable ordering; schedule sorts only when data mutates.

screens.title: Custom comparators and PlayerScore
screens.narratorSegment: When sorting objects like PlayerScore you need to define how two objects compare. The chapter shows a PlayerScore struct with an operator less-than that returns true when the left-hand score is greater, achieving descending score order. That is an idiomatic approach: either overload operator other. score makes std::sort place higher-scoring players first. A practical alternative is a lambda: std::sort(v. begin(), v. end(), [](const PlayerScore&a, const PlayerScore&b){return a. score> b. score;});. Misconceptions include thinking operator< must follow ascending numeric order — it should reflect the logical ordering you need. Another mistake is relying on implicit conversions or unstable sorts when secondary ordering matters. If you need predictable ties ordering, either include additional tie-breakers in your comparator or perform a stable sort that preserves input order for equal keys. Takeaway: define comparators that express the exact business rules for ordering, and prefer library sort calls for correctness and speed. Custom comparators and PlayerScore means provide operator< or comparator lambdas that encode your ordering rules, including tie-breakers when stability matters.. In practical terms, how to control ordering of complex objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Custom comparators
Operator< example
struct PlayerScore {
  std::string name;
  int score;
  bool operator<(const PlayerScore& other) const {
    return score > other.score; // higher scores first
  }
};

std::vector<PlayerScore> leaderboard = {{"Alice",1500},{"Bob",2000}};
std::sort(leaderboard.begin(), leaderboard.end());
Lambda alternative
std::sort(leaderboard.begin(), leaderboard.end(),
  [](const PlayerScore& a, const PlayerScore& b){
    if (a.score != b.score) return a.score > b.score; // primary key
    return a.name < b.name; // tie-breaker by name
  }
);
Use tie-breakers when required to make ordering deterministic, especially if stable ordering matters across updates.
Key Takeaway

Encode business rules in comparators and prefer explicit tie-breakers to avoid nondeterministic order for equal keys.

screens.title: Linear search and std::find
screens.narratorSegment: Linear search checks each element in turn until it finds the target or reaches the end. In C++ you often use std::find to perform this operation on a container. Linear search works on unsorted data and is straightforward to implement, which makes it useful for small or frequently changing collections. A concrete game example: checking whether a player currently holds a specific item in an unsorted inventory vector. The cost is O(N) in the worst case, so as the number of items grows, the number of comparisons increases linearly. A typical misconception is that binary search is always better — but binary search requires sorted data and often sorting a frequently changing collection is more expensive than a single linear scan. For dynamic collections where inserts and removes are frequent, a linear scan or a different data structure like a hash set may be preferable. Takeaway: use linear search for small or unsorted collections, and measure actual performance before replacing it with more complex strategies. Linear search and std::find means use linear search for unsorted or small collections; it's simple, correct, and often the most practical choice when data changes frequently.. In practical terms, when to scan every element and why it's simple but costly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Linear search & std::find
What it is
Sequentially check each element until the target is found.
std::vector<std::string> inventory = {"Sword","Shield","Potion"};
auto it = std::find(inventory.begin(), inventory.end(), "Sword");
if (it != inventory.end()) {
  // found
}
When to use it
  • Small collections where scan cost is negligible.
  • Highly dynamic collections where sorting would be more expensive than scanning.
  • Simple one-off checks in response to user actions.
Common misconception
Assuming binary search is always better; it requires sorted data and sorting costs may outweigh the benefit for dynamic data.
Key Takeaway

Linear search is simple and appropriate for many dynamic or small-scale tasks; prefer measured decisions over assumptions.

screens.title: Binary search and sorted collections
screens.narratorSegment: Binary search is a powerful technique for quickly locating an item in a sorted collection. It repeatedly halves the search interval by comparing the target to the middle element and discarding half the remaining elements on each step. That halving leads to O(log N) comparisons, which is dramatically fewer than O(N) for large N. For instance, searching a million elements requires at most about twenty comparisons with binary search, compared to up to one million with linear search. Concrete example from the chapter: std::binary_search works on a sorted vector of IDs to test membership. However, a key requirement is that the data is sorted. A common mistake is using binary search on unsorted data, which yields incorrect results. Another consideration is the cost of maintaining sort order: if your collection changes frequently, the cost to keep it sorted may outweigh binary search benefits. Use binary search when membership checks happen often and the collection is stable or easily kept sorted. Takeaway: binary search is your best friend for fast lookups in large, stable, sorted datasets. Binary search and sorted collections means use binary search for fast lookups only when data is kept sorted; otherwise its correctness and speed are compromised.. In practical terms, how halving intervals yields o(log n) performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Binary search
How it works
Repeat: compare target to middle, discard half, continue until found or interval empty.
std::vector<int> sortedIDs = {10,20,30,40,50,60};
if (std::binary_search(sortedIDs.begin(), sortedIDs.end(), 40)) {
  // found
}
When to use it
  • Large collections where membership checks are frequent.
  • Collections that are stable or cheaply kept sorted.
  • When you need O(log N) lookup behavior.
Common mistake
Forgetting to sort before calling binary search — this produces incorrect results even though the call may succeed without an error.
Key Takeaway

Binary search offers huge savings on comparisons but requires sorted input and a maintenance plan for that order.

screens.title: When to choose linear scan vs sorting + binary search
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between a linear scan and a sorted collection with binary search depends on two practical factors: how often the data changes and how often you search it. If updates are frequent — for example, items are added and removed every frame — the cost of keeping a collection sorted can exceed the savings from faster lookups. In that case, a linear scan or a hash-based structure may be better. If the data is relatively stable and searches are frequent, sorting once and using binary search yields large savings. The chapter gives a useful assessment example: finding the closest enemy to the player. Enemies can be added and removed frequently, so a single linear scan that computes the minimum distance often makes sense. Sorting by distance to pick the closest enemy would require O(N log N) to sort and then O(1) to pick the first element — but repeated sorts are expensive. Concrete decision rule: prefer linear scan for min/max queries on dynamic collections; prefer sorted+binary search for repeated membership checks on stable collections. Misconception: sorting once automatically saves cost regardless of update frequency. Always reason about mutation patterns and operation frequency before committing to a strategy. Module 5 › Chapter 4.4 › Choosing search strategy
Decision factors
  • Update frequency: how often elements are added/removed.
  • Query frequency: how often you search or check membership.
  • Collection size: small collections shift the tradeoffs toward simplicity.
Rule of thumb: linear scan for dynamic min/max; sorted+binary for repeated membership checks on stable data.
Concrete example
Finding the enemy closest to the player is best done with a linear scan updating a running minimum because enemies are often added or removed frequently. Sorting by distance each frame is more expensive than scanning.
Pitfall
Re-sorting a large vector each time an element changes when a local update or incremental structure would suffice.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Pathfinding basics: nodes, edges, and heuristics
screens.narratorSegment: Pathfinding finds a route between two points on a graph. In games that graph may be a grid, a navigation mesh, or a waypoint network. The important pieces are nodes that represent positions and edges that represent traversable connections with associated costs. Heuristics are estimates of remaining cost from a node to the goal; they are not exact but guide search toward promising options. In grid-based games Manhattan distance or Euclidean distance are common heuristics. A misconception is thinking heuristics must be exact; in A* they must instead be admissible — meaning they never overestimate the true cost to the goal — to guarantee an optimal path. Another common issue is treating pathfinding as purely visual; the algorithm's cost and heuristic choice influence both correctness and performance, especially on large maps. Concrete example: in a tile-based map where movement is orthogonal, Manhattan distance equals the minimum number of steps possible and is admissible. Takeaway: model the world as nodes and edges, pick a heuristic that reflects allowable movement, and be mindful of performance when running pathfinding frequently for many agents.

Nodes, edges, traversal costs, and heuristics. These form the input to search algorithms like A*.
Open list: nodes discovered but not fully explored.
Closed list: nodes already processed.
Heuristic: estimated cost to goal to guide search.
Heuristic example
For grid movement restricted to horizontal and vertical steps, the Manhattan distance is admissible and often efficient: abs(dx) + abs(dy).

screens.title: A* algorithm: g-cost, h-cost, and f-cost
screens.narratorSegment: A* is an informed search algorithm that selects nodes to explore based on the sum of two costs: g-cost, the actual cost from the start to the current node, and h-cost, an estimate from the current node to the goal. The priority is the f-cost, which equals g plus h. A* maintains an open list of nodes discovered but not yet fully explored, and a closed list of nodes already processed. At each step it removes the node with the smallest f-cost from the open list, explores its neighbors, and updates costs as better paths are discovered. This combination lets A* focus on promising routes while still guaranteeing optimal paths when the heuristic is admissible. A practical example: on a grid using Manhattan distance as h-cost, A* will expand nodes nearer to the goal while still accounting for actual distance traveled. A common misconception is that A* is always cheap; in large open maps with many agents, cost can add up, so consider path caching, hierarchical navigation, or limiting search depth. Takeaway: understand g, h, and f — they control both correctness and performance of A*.

Costs explained
g-cost: true cost from start to node. h-cost: heuristic estimate to goal. f-cost: g + h used to prioritize search.

On a grid that permits only orthogonal moves, use Manhattan distance as h. A* will expand nodes roughly along the corridor toward the goal while still finding the shortest path.

Running A* for many agents or on large maps can be costly; apply caching, hierarchical graphs, or limit search radii when necessary.
Key Takeaway

A* combines actual and estimated costs to focus search. Choose admissible heuristics and manage search load for many agents.

In this chapter you will build an intuitive and practical understanding of three algorithm classes that appear everywhere in games: sorting, searching, and pathfinding. You will learn why choosing the right algorithm matters for performance, how to use C++ Standard Library tools like std::sort and std::binary_search, and the basic components that make A* effective for AI navigation. Expect concrete, game-focused examples: a leaderboard sorted by score, item lookup in an inventory, and a grid-based heuristic for pathfinding. We'll explain both the mechanics and the common pitfalls so you can avoid costly mistakes like sorting every frame or using an inadmissible heuristic. By the end you will know which algorithm to reach for, how to use standard library helpers safely, and what to measure when performance becomes a concern. As you move forward, keep an eye out for the hands-on activity that walks through a ready-to-run leaderboard and binary-search inventory check — that practical step will cement these ideas.

This first objectives slide lays out the core practical skills you'll gain. First, you will understand why efficient sorting and searching matter in games. Knowing when to use a sorted collection versus a linear scan prevents costly frame-time spikes and improves responsiveness in leaderboards, rendering decisions, and inventory lookups. Second, you'll learn to use std::sort, including how to supply custom comparisons or operator overloads so complex objects like player records are sorted correctly. That skill saves time compared to hand-rolled sorts and leverages optimized introsort behavior. Third, you will differentiate linear search and binary search: you'll learn each algorithm's requirements, their typical time complexity, and scenarios where one clearly beats the other. Finally, you'll gain a conceptual grasp of pathfinding basics: open and closed lists, g-cost, h-cost, and f-cost, plus why heuristics like Manhattan distance are useful in grid-based worlds. Each objective is paired with a small competency milestone so you can verify you've achieved the skill in a practical way.

This second objectives screen focuses on applying the techniques to concrete game scenarios and recognizing common performance pitfalls. You will learn to apply sorting and searching to leaderboards and item lookup systems: how to prepare data, when to sort, and how to keep operations efficient. We'll emphasize avoiding repeated sorting inside a game loop and instead sorting only on relevant changes, a pattern that prevents unnecessary C P U usage. You will also learn to pick and implement heuristics for A* in grid-based worlds, including why admissibility matters to guarantee optimal paths. Finally, the hands-on activity included in this chapter will guide you through a leaderboard implementation and binary-search checks on an inventory vector, reinforcing both A P I usage and testing strategies. Each objective ties back to a practical milestone so you can verify your code performs correctly and efficiently in game-like scenarios.

An algorithm is simply a defined set of steps for solving a problem. In games, algorithms appear in many forms: ordering a leaderboard, searching an inventory, or choosing a path for an NPC. The key is that an algorithm specifies how inputs are processed to produce outputs. For example, when you display a leaderboard you take an unsorted list of player scores as input and produce a sorted list from highest to lowest as output. That transformation is an algorithmic process. A common misconception is that algorithms are only academic. In practice, they directly affect player experience because they determine C P U usage and latency. Another misconception is that hand-rolled implementations are always better; standard library algorithms are often faster and more robust than ad-hoc code because they are implemented and tuned for general performance. Concrete example: sorting N scores using std::sort produces an ordered vector suitable for display and rank calculations. Takeaway: treating common game tasks as algorithmic problems lets you pick proven tools that keep your code predictable and fast. What small systems in your game would you treat as algorithms first?

Sorting arranges elements into a specific order and plays a surprisingly large role in game systems. Typical uses include leaderboards that present top players, inventory screens that group and order items, rendering transparent objects back to front for correct blending, and optimizing collision broad-phase by sorting bounding boxes along an axis. Each of these examples has different constraints. Leaderboards demand a clear order by score; inventories may need stable ordering by type then name; rendering requires ordering by depth; collision systems often prefer sorts that expose nearby objects for quick elimination. A common error is to assume all tasks need the same sort behavior. Stable sorts preserve relative order of equal keys, which matters when secondary ordering is required. Performance matters: comparison-based sorts have a lower bound of O(N log N) on average, and std::sort implements a tuned hybrid commonly giving that performance in practice. Example: sort a vector of renderable objects by depth once per frame only if camera or object positions changed. Misconception to watch: sorting a very small list repeatedly costs less than complex caching, but for large collections avoid repeated full sorts. Takeaway: pick the right sort strategy and frequency for each game system to balance correctness and cost.

std::sort is the go-to C++ library function for ordering collections because it is highly optimized and typically implements an introsort: a hybrid of quicksort, heapsort, and insertion sort. The result is an algorithm that keeps average-case complexity near O(N log N) while avoiding pathological cases that can appear in simple quicksort implementations. In practical terms, that means you can rely on std::sort for most game collections: vectors of primitive values, objects with custom comparison operators, and containers where you can obtain random-access iterators. Consider the numbers and PlayerScore examples from the chapter. The numbers vector sorts in ascending order with a simple call, while PlayerScore provides either an operator< or a lambda comparator to produce descending score order. A common mistake is sorting inside a tight loop or on every frame. A better pattern is to call std::sort when data changes — for example, when a score updates, insert or update the entry and then sort if needed. Concrete example: use operator< inside PlayerScore to define default ordering for std::sort, or pass a lambda when a temporary ordering is needed. Takeaway: prefer std::sort for reliable performance and only sort when necessary.

When sorting objects like PlayerScore you need to define how two objects compare. The chapter shows a PlayerScore struct with an operator less-than that returns true when the left-hand score is greater, achieving descending score order. That is an idiomatic approach: either overload operator other. score makes std::sort place higher-scoring players first. A practical alternative is a lambda: std::sort(v. begin(), v. end(), [](const PlayerScore&a, const PlayerScore&b){return a. score> b. score;});. Misconceptions include thinking operator< must follow ascending numeric order — it should reflect the logical ordering you need. Another mistake is relying on implicit conversions or unstable sorts when secondary ordering matters. If you need predictable ties ordering, either include additional tie-breakers in your comparator or perform a stable sort that preserves input order for equal keys. Takeaway: define comparators that express the exact business rules for ordering, and prefer library sort calls for correctness and speed. Linear search works on unsorted data and is straightforward to implement, which makes it useful for small or frequently changing collections. A concrete game example: checking whether a player currently holds a specific item in an unsorted inventory vector. The cost is O(N) in the worst case, so as the number of items grows, the number of comparisons increases linearly. A typical misconception is that binary search is always better — but binary search requires sorted data and often sorting a frequently changing collection is more expensive than a single linear scan. Takeaway: use linear search for small or unsorted collections, and measure actual performance before replacing it with more complex strategies.
